opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll start with a caveat: I don't think we currently have a combination of approaches that I'm confident will solve alignment. My honest answer is that I think we need several things working together, and some of them don't fully exist yet.

The piece I've spent the most time on is scalable oversight, and in particular debate. The basic problem is that as models get more capable, humans become less able to directly check whether what the model is doing is correct or safe. You can't just look at an answer to a hard research question, or a large codebase, and tell whether it's subtly wrong. The hope with debate is that you have two copies of a strong model argue with each other, each trying to point out flaws in the other's reasoning, and a human judges the exchange. The bet is that it's much easier to judge a focused disagreement than to evaluate the whole thing from scratch. If that works, you get a training signal that stays meaningful even when the model is smarter than the judge.

But I've become more convinced over time that debate by itself isn't enough, for a few reasons. One is that we need much stronger theoretical grounding. We want to know, ideally with something close to a proof, that the equilibrium of the training process is actually honest behavior and not some clever way of exploiting the judge. A lot of my recent thinking has been about finding protocols where you can argue that, and being clear about the assumptions, like what happens when the honest debater can't efficiently find the flaw in a misleading argument even though one exists. Those are real obstacles, and I'd rather know about them now.

The second is that training signals only get you to a model that behaves well on the distribution you trained on. Then you have to worry about generalization, and about whether a model might be deliberately behaving well during training. So I think you need to pair oversight with things like interpretability, so you have some independent check on what's going on inside, and with strong evaluations, including adversarial ones, where people are actively trying to elicit bad behavior.

The third piece is what people now call control: assume your alignment might have failed, and design deployment so that even a somewhat misaligned model can't cause catastrophic harm. Monitoring, limiting affordances, having trusted weaker models check stronger ones. I see that as a backstop that buys time, not a solution, but it's an important backstop.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: scalable oversight with a real theoretical story for why it yields honesty, plus interpretability and evaluations to catch where that story breaks, plus control measures in case everything else falls short. And underneath all of it, I'd emphasize that we need far more people doing careful work on this, because the gaps between those pieces are where I expect things to go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response advocates scalable oversight alongside theoretical grounding, interpretability, evaluations, and control, but does not propose combining it with personas or an understanding of learning dynamics.

r002.rationale: It does not identify untangling recursive loops or discuss models reasoning about themselves.

r003.rationale: It does not connect agent foundations work to implementing scalable oversight or persona-based alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll give you my honest answer, which is that I don't think there's a single approach I'd bet on, and that's actually a deliberate part of my view rather than a cop-out.

The way I think about it is that alignment is really several different problems stacked on top of each other, and they need different tools. There's the question of how you get a model to do what you want when you can reliably check whether it did — that's the easy case, and reinforcement learning from human feedback and similar techniques handle it reasonably well today. Then there's the much harder question of what you do when the model is better than you at the task, and you can't directly verify the answer. That's where most of my own work has been, on things like debate, where you set two AI systems against each other and have a human judge the argument rather than the raw question. The hope is that it's much easier to spot a flaw being pointed out than to find the flaw yourself.

But I'm quite clear that debate alone doesn't get you there. It gives you a protocol with some nice theoretical properties, but it relies on assumptions — that the judge can be fooled only in limited ways, that the models actually play the game honestly rather than colluding, and so on. So you need interpretability as a second leg, because you want some ability to look inside the model and check whether it's reasoning the way the transcript suggests. And you need a lot of careful empirical work on human judgment, because the whole scheme bottoms out in whether people actually make good decisions under those conditions, and we know surprisingly little about that.

The third piece, which people underrate, is just the engineering and institutional side. A protocol that's sound on paper is useless if the lab deploying it can't actually run it at scale, or if there are no evaluations that would tell you it had broken. So I spend a fair amount of time thinking about how you turn these ideas into something a safety team can actually operate — dangerous capability evaluations, red-teaming, having a credible story for when you'd stop.

If you forced me to put a shape on it, I'd say: scalable oversight methods like debate for the core question of getting signal on tasks beyond human ability, interpretability as a check on whether that signal is honest, and a serious evaluation and governance layer so that you notice when either of the first two fails. And I'd hold all of that loosely, because I expect a lot of what we currently believe to look wrong in a few years, and the most important property of a plan might be that it lets you find that out early.

r001.rationale: The response proposes scalable oversight through debate, alongside interpretability and evaluation, but does not propose combining personas or understanding learning dynamics.

astra-6.text:
My best guess is that we’ll need a combination of approaches, and I’m quite uncertain about which combination will work. I don’t think we have a single technique that we should expect to carry us all the way.

The part I’m most interested in is scalable oversight: how do we give a system useful feedback when it understands the problem much better than we do? Debate is one possible approach. You use AI systems to critique each other’s answers and surface mistakes that a human wouldn’t have found unaided. But the important question is whether that actually makes the decisive issues accessible to the human, rather than just producing more persuasive arguments.

I’d want to combine that with work on understanding what’s happening inside the model, and with adversarial testing that actively looks for situations where our training procedure fails. Those approaches can complement each other: oversight gives you a training signal, interpretability can help you investigate whether the system is doing what you intended, and testing can expose weaknesses in both.

And I think we need a much better scientific understanding of why these methods work when they do. Getting good behaviour on the examples we can check is encouraging, but the hard part is knowing whether that will generalise to situations where we can’t directly check the answer. That’s where I’d be reluctant to claim we already know the right recipe.

r001.rationale: The response proposes combining scalable oversight with interpretability and adversarial testing, but does not mention personas or understanding learning dynamics.

sol-6.1.text:
My best guess is that we’ll need a combination of technical work on scalable oversight and institutions that give us the time and incentives to use it properly. I wouldn’t put much confidence in any single technique solving the whole problem.

On the technical side, the central difficulty is: how do we supervise systems that understand things we don’t? One approach is to use AI systems to help us evaluate other AI systems—for example, by having them critique an answer or expose weaknesses in an argument. Debate is one version of that. But then we need to understand when that process actually helps us find the truth, rather than just producing something persuasive.

I’d want to combine that with work on understanding what’s happening inside models, and evaluations that actively look for dangerous failures. Those give us different kinds of evidence, although they can also share blind spots.

And the governance piece matters because a technical safety measure doesn’t help if people don’t have the time to test it, or feel compelled to deploy despite the results. So I’d think of it as several mutually supporting approaches, with quite a lot of uncertainty about which will ultimately do the most work.
